title: Where August's river comes from
teaches: Groundwater in the spaces between grains, Darcy's law, baseflow, and gaining and losing streams
summary: **Groundwater fills the spaces between grains.** Under western Washington it is almost never an underground lake or river: it sits in the pores of sand and gravel and in cracks in rock.
**The water table is where the pores fill up.** Above it the ground holds air and some water; below it every pore is full, and a well fills to its level.

**Darcy's law: flow follows the drop in head.** Double the drop across a layer and the flow doubles; double the thickness and it halves; and each material has its own conductivity, from free-flowing gravel to almost sealed clay.
**Groundwater is slow.** In sand it creeps a fraction of a metre a day, so water reaching a river may have fallen as rain years before.
**Baseflow is the river the ground supplies.** A gaining stream is fed through its bed and banks wherever the water table stands above it, and in a dry August that seep is nearly all the river.

**Snow decides when the ground is refilled.** In 2015 a normal amount of precipitation fell as rain, ran off in winter, and left the aquifers draining from February, so rivers reached record lows by August.

**A well can turn a gaining creek into a losing one.** Where the water table lies below the bed a stream leaks into the ground, and a well beside a creek tips it that way once it takes more than the baseflow feeding that stretch, which happens sooner as summer goes on.

**On islands fresh water floats on salt.** For every metre the water table stands above sea level, fresh water reaches about 40 metres below, so overpumping near the shore draws salt water up into wells.

parts.title: A normal winter, a dry river

blocks.text: The winter of 2014 to 2015 did not look like the start of a drought. Rain gauges in western Washington collected close to their usual totals between November and March, and the rivers ran high through the winter storms. What was missing was the cold. Storm after storm came in warm, so precipitation that normally falls as snow in the Cascades and the Olympics fell as rain and ran straight off. On 1 April, the date snow surveyors use to take the measure of the year's store, the mountain snowpack was a small fraction of normal, and in parts of the Olympics there was almost none.

In May the governor declared a drought across the whole state. By August many rivers in western Washington were running at or near the lowest flows ever measured for the time of year, and some small lowland creeks had shrunk to pools. Newspapers called it a snow drought: a drought in a year with a normal amount of rain.

Lesson 1 described the snowpack as a reservoir that holds winter's water until summer. That accounts for the rivers in May, June and July of a normal year. It does not account for August and September, when the snow below the high peaks has long since melted and weeks go by with hardly any rain, and yet the rivers keep running. Snoqualmie Falls, which roars in February, thins to a fraction of itself by late summer, but it never stops. Something keeps feeding it. This lesson follows that water underground, and then comes back to 2015.

**The underground lake.** Ask someone to draw groundwater and you will often get a cave: a dark lake under the hills, or a stream running through a tunnel in the rock. Such places exist, in limestone country where water has dissolved channels through the rock, but they are rare, and there are almost none under western Washington. Nearly all groundwater is somewhere less dramatic: in the spaces between grains of sand and gravel, and in the cracks of solid rock.

Fill a jar with gravel and pour water in. A jar that looks full of stone takes a surprising amount, about a third of its volume. That share of empty space is the material's **porosity**. Clean sand and gravel have porosities of about 25 to 40 percent. Clay, made of flakes far smaller than sand grains, is more porous still, often half water, but as the next part shows it lets that water through only very slowly. Underground, below a certain depth, all that space is already full of water: a hillside of saturated gravel is roughly a third water, held in countless small connected rooms.

Dig down from the surface and the pores change. Near the top they hold some air and some water clinging to the grains, like a sponge that has been wrung out. Lower down every pore is full. The surface where the full zone begins is the [[water table|ground]]: dig a hole below it and water seeps in from the sides until it stands at that level, and no higher. A layer of sediment or rock that holds water and lets it move freely enough to supply a well, as clean sand and gravel do and clay does not, is an **aquifer**.

blocks.caption: Groundwater lives in the pores. Above the water table the pores hold air and water; below it they are full, and a well fills to that level. Clay holds the most water of the three, but its pores are so small that the water barely moves.

blocks.text: Under the Puget lowland the best aquifers were laid down by ice. When the Vashon glacier, the last ice sheet to cover the lowland, pushed south about 17,000 years ago, its meltwater spread broad sheets of clean sand and gravel, called **outwash**, in front of it. The ice then rode over the outwash and plastered it with a dense, compacted mix of clay, sand and stones, glacial **till**, which Seattle gardeners call hardpan because a spade bounces off it. Till passes water slowly, so it acts as a lid. Many of the region's wells go down through the till to reach the outwash beneath it.

Henry Darcy was the chief engineer of Dijon, in Burgundy, a town that had long been short of clean water. In the 1830s and 1840s he brought it spring water through a covered aqueduct about 12 kilometres long, piped to fountains in the streets. In 1856 he described the system in a long book, *Les Fontaines publiques de la ville de Dijon* (The Public Fountains of the City of Dijon). The part that made his name is in an appendix.

The town wanted to filter its water through beds of sand, and Darcy needed to know how big a filter would have to be. In 1855, with the engineer Charles Ritter, he set up an upright iron pipe about 2.5 metres tall and 35 centimetres across, put a layer of sand in it, and ran water down through the sand. Two gauges, glass tubes part filled with mercury that the water pressure pushed up, showed the pressure above and below the sand. He changed how thick the sand was and how hard the water was pushed, and timed how much came out at the bottom.

What drives the water is best measured as **head**: the height to which water would rise in an open tube connected to that point.[^head] Water underground always moves from high head to low. The figure is Darcy's column, starting with a 1 metre drop in head across a metre of coarse sand. Its slider sets the drop, from 0.2 to 3 metres, and chips choose the grain. Before you move it, guess what doubling the drop to 2 metres does to the flow out of the bottom.

blocks.caption: Darcy's column: water runs down through a metre of sand, pushed by the drop in head between the gauge above the sand and the gauge below it. The plot shows the flow out of the bottom. Choose the grain and set the drop.
blocks.task: Guess, then set the drop to 2 m

blocks.text: Darcy's result was that simple. The flow is proportional to the drop in head across the sand, and inversely proportional to the sand's thickness: double the drop and the flow doubles, double the thickness and it halves. A wider pipe passes more, in proportion to its area. And each material has its own number for how easily water passes through it, its **hydraulic conductivity**, written K. In symbols, flow = K × area × drop in head ÷ thickness. This is **Darcy's law**, and every groundwater calculation since rests on it.[^law]

Switch the grain chips from gravel to clay. Water passes through clean gravel about ten million times more easily than through clay. Clay is porous, often more so than sand, but its pores are so small that the water clings to the flakes and barely moves.[^clay] That is why a layer of clay or till can hold up the water in the sand above it, or seal in an aquifer below.

**How fast is groundwater?** The water table usually slopes gently, a metre or so of drop in every hundred metres. Put that slope into Darcy's law for clean sand, with K about a ten-thousandth of a metre a second, and divide by the share of the ground that is open pore, about a third, since the water only moves through the pores. It creeps along at about a third of a metre a day, roughly 100 metres a year. Rain that soaks in two kilometres from a river can take twenty years to reach it. The river carries the same water two kilometres in under an hour.

blocks.caption: How far water moves in a day: typical groundwater for a water table sloping 1 metre in 100, and a lowland river for comparison. Each step on the scale is ten times the last; real aquifers vary several times either way.

parts.title: The water table meets the river

blocks.text: The water table is not flat. It rises under hills, where rain soaks in, and falls toward valleys, following the shape of the land in a smoothed-out way. Groundwater moves from high head to low, as Darcy's law says it must, which near the surface means roughly down the water table's slope. In a valley the lowest head is the river. Wherever the water table stands above the river's surface, groundwater seeps into the channel through its bed and banks, along every metre of its length. A river fed this way is a **gaining stream**, and the water it gains is [[baseflow|ground]].

Lesson 2's hydrograph showed a river rising quickly after a storm and then falling back along a long, slowly flattening tail. The quick part is the storm's own rain running off the land. The tail is baseflow: the aquifers along the valley draining into the river, more and more slowly as their water tables sink. After weeks without rain it is all that is left. In a dry August nearly all the water in a lowland river has come out of the ground, and much of it fell as rain months or years before.

That is also why creeks feel so cold in August. Ten metres down, the ground hardly notices the seasons and stays near the year's average air temperature, about 10 °C (50 °F) in the Puget lowland. Groundwater seeps out at that temperature, while the surface of a shallow August creek can warm past 20 °C in the sun, so the seeps are the coldest water in the river, and trout and salmon gather where they come in.

Now back to 2015. In a normal year the snow melts from April into July. Some of the melt runs straight into the rivers, and much of it soaks into the soil and gravel of the mountain valleys, topping up their aquifers just before the dry season begins. In 2015 the same water arrived as rain through the winter, when the ground was already full, so most of it ran off at once, raising winter floods instead of summer stores. With no snowmelt to refill them in spring, the aquifers started draining in late winter instead of early summer. By August their water tables, and the rivers they feed, had fallen to record lows.

Not every river gains. Where the water table lies below the riverbed, water leaks out of the channel into the ground, and the river shrinks as it flows. That is a **losing stream**. Many rivers in dry country lose water for much of their length, and some sink into their own gravel in summer. In western Washington most rivers gain, but a reach can switch. A creek crossing a fan of coarse gravel at a mountain front may lose water there and gain it back lower down, and in a long dry spell a small creek can go from gaining to losing as the water table beside it falls.

People can switch it too. A well beside a creek pumps from the same aquifer that feeds the creek, and lowers the water table around itself in a cone. At first the well draws on water stored in the ground nearby. As pumping goes on the cone spreads until it reaches the creek, and from then on every litre the well lifts is taken from the creek: first as baseflow that no longer arrives, and, once the well takes more than all of that, as creek water drawn out through its bed. Hydrologists call this **capture**. The figure is a valley in cross-section: a creek at the foot of a rock wall, an aquifer rising away from it, and a well.

blocks.caption: A creek, its aquifer and a well, in cross-section. Set the weeks since the last soaking rain (0 to 16) and the well's pumping (0 to 40 litres a second). The arrow at the bank shows which way water crosses it, into the creek or out of it. A model, after the pumping has run long enough (weeks to years) for the water table to stop changing.
blocks.task: Guess, then pump until the creek loses water

blocks.text: The creek turns from gaining to losing once the well takes more than the ground was feeding that stretch of creek. That threshold falls as summer goes on, because baseflow falls with the water table. Set the pumping to 15 litres a second and press Play to run the weeks: in June the ground feeds the creek 60 litres a second and the well takes a quarter of it, but by mid-September the creek is losing water. Washington's Supreme Court and legislature took up exactly this question in 2016 and 2018.[^hirst]

**On a bluff.** After a wet spell, walk a beach below one of the high bluffs on the Sound, at Discovery Park, Carkeek Park or along the Whidbey shore, on a falling tide so the water cannot trap you. Keep well out from the foot of the bluff: look from the water's edge, and stay away altogether after heavy rain, when slides are most likely. Partway up the face, look for a line of dark wet ground, moss, ferns or trickles. That line is often where water soaking down through sand meets a layer of clay it cannot pass and runs out sideways: a **perched** water table, held up on the clay above the main one, seen edge-on in the bluff. Seep lines like these are where many of Seattle's landslides begin.

On an island the aquifer has salt water on every side. Rain soaking into Whidbey, Camano or the San Juan Islands forms a lens of fresh water that floats on the seawater filling the ground below sea level, the way oil floats on vinegar. Fresh water is only about 2.5 percent lighter than seawater, so the lens floats deep, the way most of an iceberg sits below the waterline: to balance, a column of fresh water must be about 40 times longer below sea level than above it. So for every metre the water table stands above sea level, the fresh water reaches about 40 metres below it.[^lens] The same rule works in reverse. Pump a well near the shore hard enough to lower the water table by a metre, and the boundary with the salt water beneath rises by about 40 metres, straight up toward the bottom of the well. Wells along island shores are watched for this, **seawater intrusion**, because once a well turns salty it can stay that way for years.

East of the mountains, Spokane drinks from the opposite extreme. Its aquifer lies in boulders and gravel dumped by the Ice Age floods that swept eastern Washington, and water moves through it metres a day, far faster than through Puget lowland sand. Even there it is water moving through the spaces between stones; the stones are large, and so are the spaces.

blocks.caption: Six questions on groundwater and baseflow
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Which picture of groundwater under western Washington is closest to the truth?
choices: Water filling the pores between grains of sand and gravel, and cracks in rock
Lakes and streams running through caves and tunnels in the bedrock
Slow underground rivers that follow the same valleys as the rivers above
items.why: Nearly all groundwater sits in pores and cracks. Underground lakes and rivers need rock that dissolves, such as limestone, and are rare here.

items.ask: Water drains through a sand filter at 6 litres a minute when the water above it stands 1 metre higher than the outlet. It is raised to stand 2 metres higher, and nothing else changes. What is the new flow?
choices: About 6 litres a minute; the sand sets the rate
items.why: Darcy's law: the flow through a porous layer is proportional to the drop in head across it, and inversely proportional to the layer's thickness.

items.ask: A lowland river is still running after six weeks without rain in August. Where is most of its water coming from?
choices: Groundwater seeping into the channel from aquifers along the valley
Snow still melting on the low and middle slopes of the mountains
Rain from the last storm still draining out of the hillside soils
items.why: That is baseflow. Surface runoff is gone within days of a storm, and by August the snow below the high peaks has melted; the ground drains for months.

items.ask: In the winter of 2014 to 2015 western Washington had near-normal precipitation, yet many rivers ran at record lows the next August. Which explanation is best?
choices: Rain fell instead of snow and ran off in winter, so no spring melt refilled the aquifers
The warm winter dried the soil, so most of the rain evaporated before soaking in
A hot summer drew far more water from the rivers for farms and cities than usual
items.why: The total was close to normal, but it came at the wrong time. Without snowmelt in spring, the aquifers that feed summer baseflow began draining months early.

items.ask: A well beside a creek pumps steadily for months. When does that stretch of creek start losing water to the ground?
choices: When its pumping exceeds the baseflow the ground was feeding that stretch
As soon as the pump starts, whatever rate it runs at
When the cone of lowered water table first reaches the creek bed
items.why: Once the cone reaches the creek, the well's water comes out of the creek's baseflow. If the well takes more than all of that baseflow, the rest is drawn out of the creek through its bed, so the creek loses water.

items.ask: Why can heavy pumping near the shore of an island turn a well salty?
choices: Fresh water floats on salt water underground, and lowering it lets the salt rise far more
Seawater soaks down through the beach at high tide and flows inland to the well
Pumping draws in old seawater trapped in the clay layers since the Ice Age
items.why: Fresh water is about 2.5 percent lighter than seawater, so the fresh lens floats about 40 times as deep below sea level as the water table stands above it.

head.title: Head
head.text: The height in an open tube counts two things at once: how high the point is, and how hard the water there is pressed, since pressure pushes water up the tube. Water deep under a hill, pressed by all the water above it, can stand higher in a tube than water at a valley floor, so groundwater can flow sideways or even upward into the bed of a river. It always flows from high head to low; near the surface that is usually downhill.

law.title: Darcy's law in symbols
law.text: Q = K × A × Δh ÷ L: the flow Q (cubic metres a second) equals the conductivity K (metres a second) times the area A (square metres) times the drop in head Δh (metres), divided by the thickness L (metres). A typical K is about 1 centimetre a second for clean gravel, a hundredth to a thousandth of that for clean sand, and a billionth or less for clay. Darcy's law holds while the water creeps; in very coarse gravel with a steep drop the flow turns eddying and the law begins to fail.

clay.title: Why clay holds water and keeps it
clay.text: Clay particles are flakes thousandths of a millimetre across, and the gaps between them are smaller still. Water in such narrow gaps is held by its attraction to the flakes' surfaces, so a clay can be half water by volume and still pass almost none of it.

hirst.title: The Hirst decision
hirst.text: In 2016, in Whatcom County v. Hirst, the Washington Supreme Court ruled that a county could not approve a new house supplied by a household well without first checking that the well would not take water from streams that state rules guarantee a minimum flow. Building in rural areas stalled until the legislature passed the Streamflow Restoration Act in 2018. New household wells are allowed again, with a fee and a daily limit on use, and each watershed must plan projects that put back roughly what the wells capture.

lens.title: Forty to one
lens.text: This is the Ghyben-Herzberg rule, found by Willem Badon Ghyben in the Netherlands in the 1880s and Alexander Herzberg in Germany in 1901. Seawater is about 1.025 times as dense as fresh water, so a column of fresh water balances a column of seawater 1/40 shorter: each metre of fresh water above sea level holds the boundary about 40 metres down. Real lenses blur into the salt water through a zone of mixing at their base, so the rule is a rough estimate of where the boundary lies.
